item.title: The Daily Star – How Sufism and shrine veneration shaped Muslim society in the Bengal delta
item.description:
The process of Islamisation in the Bengal delta was complex, shaped by the region’s pre-existing religious and cultural beliefs and practices. Early Sufis and mystics played a significant role in spreading Islam throughout the region. By establishing khanqahs (Sufi lodges), dargahs (shrines), and mosques, early Sufis helped mediate the relationship between Islamic teachings and the diverse religious and cultural environment. Shrine-centred devotional practices, the veneration of pirs (spiritual masters), and the circulation of vernacular religious literature contributed to the emergence of distinctive forms of Bengali Muslim religious expression.

It has been argued that, even before the establishment of Mughal hegemony, there was scarcely a locality in Bengal without a shrine. A fifteenth-century letter attributed to Mir Sayyid Ashraf Jahangir Simnani (d. 1425), addressed to Sultan Ibrahim Sharqi of Jaunpur (d. 1440?), captures the extent of Sufi influence in Bengal: "In short, in the country of Bengal, what to speak of the cities, there is no town and no village where holy saints did not come and settle down" (quoted in Karim, Social History of the Muslims in Bengal (Down to A. D. 1538), 1985, p. 116). Although this statement should be understood as a representation of the widespread reputation of Sufi saints rather than a literal demographic record, it illustrates the significance attributed to their presence in the region.

The widespread veneration of Sufi saints has frequently led scholars to associate the Islamisation of the Bengal delta with Sufi missionary activity. Yet the historical formation of Muslim society cannot be explained through conversion narratives alone. It involved political transformations, agrarian expansion, settlement patterns, institutional developments, religious encounters, and the production of new forms of religious knowledge. This paper examines these interconnected processes through the historical development of Sufism and shrine-centred religious practices in Bengal. Drawing particularly on the works of Asim Roy, Richard M. Eaton, and Ayesha A. Irani, it argues that Bengali Islam emerged through the interaction of social and geographical transformations, localised religious practices, and vernacular intellectual production.

The geographical territories that constitute the Bengal delta were historically divided into several overlapping regions, including Raṛḥa, Gauṛa, Vanga, Samatata, Harikela, Pundra, and Varendra (Ramesh C. Majumdar, 1971, History of Ancient Bengal; Niharranjan Ray, 1949, Bangalir Itihas: Adi Parbo). Archaeological evidence suggests that Bengal was inhabited from prehistoric times, while its population and cultural formations developed through successive migrations, political expansions, and interactions among indigenous and external communities.

The region experienced several phases of political consolidation before the arrival of Muslim rulers. Chandragupta, the Pala ruler Gopala, and the Sena ruler Vijayasena each contributed to the political integration of parts of Bengal at different historical moments. The conquest of Bengal by Ikhtiyaruddin Muhammad bin Bakhtiyar Khalji in 1204 marked the beginning of sustained Muslim political dominance in the region. It also facilitated the movement of Muslim scholars, administrators, merchants, preachers, and wandering dervishes into Bengal. Nevertheless, the expansion of Islam was neither immediate nor uniform. The emergence of Muslim communities was a prolonged process involving political authority, institutional patronage, settlement, agrarian development, and religious interaction.

Muslim contact with Bengal, however, predated the establishment of Muslim political dominance. Arab merchants visited the coastal regions of the Bay of Bengal from the early medieval period, and commercial networks may have facilitated the circulation of Islamic ideas and practices. Some scholars have also suggested that Muslim religious figures visited or settled in Bengal before the thirteenth-century conquest, although the chronology and historical evidence associated with several early Sufi figures remain uncertain.

Among the figures traditionally associated with the early history of Sufism in Bengal are Shah Sultan Rumi, Shaikh Ahmad or Abbas ibn Hamza Nishapuri, Shah Sultan Balkhi, Baba Adam Shahid, Shah Makhdum, and Shaykh Jalal al-Din Tabrizi. Regional traditions associate Shah Sultan Rumi with Netrakona, Shah Sultan Balkhi with Bogra, Shah Makhdum with Rajshahi, and Baba Adam Shahid with Vikrampura. Shaykh Jalal al-Din Tabrizi, associated with the Suhrawardiyya order, is traditionally connected with the early establishment of Sufi networks in Bengal. These accounts demonstrate the importance of saintly genealogies and local memory in the construction of Bengal's sacred geography, although individual dates and details of these figures' lives require careful historical verification.

The relationship between local religio-cultural traditions and the process of Islamisation in Bengal has been interpreted through several complementary historical, literary, and anthropological approaches. Asim Roy's The Islamic Syncretistic Tradition in Bengal (1983) focuses on the cultural and religious processes through which Islam developed a distinctive Bengali expression.

Roy argues that Bengali Islam emerged through sustained interaction between Islamic religious traditions and the existing cultural and religious practices of Bengal. In describing the process of Islamisation, he holds that it was a “social and cultural process operating in Bengal, where Islam was not a primary but a secondary culture, that is, exogenous and not endogenous to the particular region, and also where Islam is not a single or the only great tradition since it entered a land which was not culturally virgin, and confronted the long-established endogenous Hindu great tradition” (p. 4). Within this framework, Sufi saints and Bengali Muslim literary figures served as cultural intermediaries. Pirs helped connect Islamic religious authority with popular understandings of spiritual power, while vernacular writers translated Islamic narratives and concepts into familiar linguistic and cultural forms.

Roy also associates the development of pir-centred religious culture with the environmental and economic conditions of the delta. The frequent changes in river courses, displacement of settlements, and uncertainties of agrarian life created circumstances in which people sought spiritual protection and assistance. Pirs consequently became important figures in the popular religious imagination. He observes that Bengali Muslim folk culture developed an extensive pantheon of pirs to whom people turned in times of hardship and uncertainty (1983, p. 51).

Roy's interpretation is particularly significant for its attention to punthi literature, a tradition of Bengali manuscript-based religious and narrative writing. Such literature incorporated Islamic narratives, prophetic histories, local legends, and familiar literary conventions. Its authors helped establish a Bengali medium for expressing Islamic religious ideas and connecting them with the experiences of local communities. Their work as cultural mediators involved combining Islamic traditions with local cultural practices, which ultimately gave Bengali Islam a syncretistic character that persisted until the emergence of various revivalist movements in the nineteenth century (p. 251).

However, Roy's interpretation of syncretism has generated scholarly debate. His framework has been criticised for potentially assuming that the indigenous population was predominantly Hindu, for insufficiently differentiating between Buddhist and other local traditions, and for underestimating the independent spiritual appeal of Sufi piety. His emphasis on the relationship between changing river courses, land settlement, and the popularity of pirs may also be insufficient to explain the emergence of Muslim communities in areas where these environmental conditions were less directly influential. These limitations have been discussed by Eaton (The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, 1204–1760, 1993, p. 289; Essays on Islam and Indian History, 2000, p. 270), Rashiduzzaman (1994, “Islam, Muslim identity and nationalism in Bangladesh,” p. 47), and Harder (Sufism and Saint Veneration in Contemporary Bangladesh: The Maijbhandaris of Chittagong, 2011, p. 325), and especially by Tony K. Stewart (“In Search of Equivalence: Conceiving Muslim-Hindu Encounter Through Translation Theory,” History of Religions, 40:3, 2001, pp. 260–287), who argues that Muslim writers did not create a syncretic religion by blending Hindu and Islamic beliefs but rather attempted to find approximate equivalents in local religious or shared vernacular vocabularies to express a distinct Islamic worldview.

Regarding Roy’s interpretation, Ayesha A. Irani (2021) suggests that vernacular authors were not necessarily seeking to absorb or assimilate Islam into pre-existing indigenous religious traditions. Their use of familiar literary forms and theological vocabulary could also serve to articulate, communicate, and establish Islamic scriptural knowledge within Bengali society.

While Roy emphasises cultural mediation and syncretism, Richard M. Eaton's The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, 1204–1760 (1993) offers an especially influential explanation by connecting the expansion of Muslim society with the transformation of the Bengal delta's agrarian frontier.
 
Cover of Richard M. Eaton’s seminal book The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, 1204–1760 (University of California Press, 1996 paperback edition).

Eaton challenges explanations that attribute the spread of Islam primarily to military conquest, mass immigration, political coercion, or the attraction of an allegedly egalitarian Islamic social order. Instead, he locates the expansion of Muslim society within the eastward movement of agricultural settlement, particularly the clearing of forests and the development of rice cultivation in eastern Bengal, facilitated by changes in river courses.

His interpretation identifies three interconnected frontiers: the political frontier, associated with the expansion of Muslim political authority; the agrarian frontier, characterised by forest clearance, settlement, and agricultural expansion; and the Islamic frontier, through which local populations gradually became incorporated into Muslim religious communities. These processes reinforced one another, although they did not necessarily occur simultaneously or uniformly. The growth of Muslim societies, he argues, correlated with the adoption of sedentary agriculture with the help of the Sufis (Islamic History as Global History, 1990, p. 35).

He observes that between the sixteenth and twentieth centuries, the authority of charismatic Sufis in Bengal rested on three overlapping bases: their connection with the forest, their connection with the supernatural world, and their connection with mosques through which they were believed to institutionalise the cult of Islam (1993, p. 218). In fact, Islamisation involved the displacement of local superhuman agencies by Islamic ones (1993, p. 282). Eaton also observes that the common elements in the perceptions of superhuman agencies in both indigenous and Islamic cosmologies helped the Sufis gain acceptance among Hindu and Buddhist communities. Allah was perceived as the high God, followed by superhuman agents, such as the Prophet Muhammad at the upper end of the spiritual hierarchy, and various pirs (spiritual preceptors), with their charismatic powers, at the lower end. This hierarchy was so familiar to the indigenous non-Muslim population that they did not perceive Islam as an alien belief system. He contends that the Sufis' engagement in expanding arable land made Islam synonymous with agrarian growth. In fact, he argues, the growth of Muslim societies correlated with the adoption of sedentary agriculture (1990, p. 35). Thus, Islam was perceived culturally by the local population as a civilisation-building ideology and, as such, was not viewed as an alien tradition (1993, p. 310).

Early pioneers of Islam, both Sufi and non-Sufi, took advantage, in some cases, of the incentives offered by Muslim rulers in the form of land grants for clearing forests to expand rice cultivation. While non-Sufi preachers established mosques and madrasas, Sufi preachers and their followers established not only mosques but also khanqahs and dargahs. These institutions fostered both the formal and spiritual aspects of Islam, and together they contributed to the emergence of an Islamic culture. Alongside the expansion of arable land and the agrarian way of life, a locally structured form of Islam, increasingly infused with the culture of saints and saint veneration, gave rise to large Muslim communities in Bengal (1990, p. 36).
 
The Sixty Dome Mosque in Bagerhat, built by the Sufi saint and general Khan Jahan Ali in the 15th century, stands as a testament to the historical expansion of Islam in the Bengal delta. Photo: Moaz Mahmud/Wikimedia Commons

Muslim rulers, particularly the Mughals, were interested not in religious conversion but rather in revenue extraction through land grant policies aimed at expanding arable land by clearing forests. Eaton observes that Mughal administrators frequently distinguished political governance from religious proselytisation. He observes that Muslim rulers, especially “the Mughals were determined not to allow religion to interfere with their administration in Bengal” (2001, p. 31) and did not promote the conversion of Bengalis to Islam. He holds, “Regarding the religion of Mughal ashraf, three features stand out: (a) a special link with the pan-Indian Chishti Order, (b) a conceptual separation of religion and state, and (c) a disinclination to convert Bengalis to Islam” (2001, p. 28). This interpretation complicates the assumption that Muslim political authority automatically produced religious conversion.

Rafiuddin Ahmed (The Bengali Muslims 1871–1906: A Quest for Identity, 2001, p. 12) similarly emphasises the relationship between Muslim institutional expansion and the acculturation of local cultivating communities. He argues that Muslim rulers established mosques and madrasas, supported Islamic scholars and preachers, endowed religious institutions, and appointed qazis. These developments contributed to the gradual expansion of Muslim society, particularly through the incorporation of new agricultural communities.

Taken together, Eaton and Ahmed demonstrate that the historical formation of Muslim society in Bengal involved more than the preaching of religious doctrines. It was embedded in the transformation of land, settlement, institutions, and everyday social relations. Sufis were important participants in this process, but their activities operated alongside those of rulers, administrators, scholars, merchants, and non-Sufi religious figures.

Ayesha A. Irani's The Muhammad Avatāra: Salvation History, Translation, and the Making of Bengali Islam (2021) extends the discussion of Bengali Islamisation by examining the relationship between translation, religious imagination, and the production of Islamic knowledge. Her study focuses particularly on the seventeenth-century Bengali Muslim poet Saiyad Sultan and his Nabīvaṃśa (The Lineage of the Prophets). Drawing on the Arabo-Persian tradition of the Tales of the Prophets (qisas an-nabiya), the work presents Islamic salvation history through Bengali literary conventions and conceptual frameworks familiar to its audience.

Irani demonstrates that the Nabīvaṃśa reflects extensive intellectual and literary exchanges among Muslim, Vaiṣṇava, Nātha, and haṭhayoga traditions. These exchanges reveal common features shared by both Muslim and non-Muslim communities. As Irani observes, they “share a host of these and other common features—theological, narratological, aesthetic, rhetorical, and linguistic—suggests that they participated in overlapping polysystems of performance and reception, of Sufism, Nātha doctrine, haṭhayoga, and Kṛṣṇa bhakti, of orally and textually, evidence of, among other things, the fluency of the circulation of ideas and peoples in the premodern period” (p. 33).

Irani further interprets the Nabīvaṃśa as an example of what she describes as a "Purāṇa-Korān" tradition. In this literary framework, Saiyad Sultan reconstructs prophetic history through a narrative that incorporates pre-Ādamic prophets, Hindu religious figures, and Indic sacred texts into an Islamic account of salvation. The narrative's recurring motif of the earth's appeal for divine intervention provides a framework for connecting different religious histories and establishing Muhammad's prophetic significance (p. 195). It also illustrates the integration of Qurʾānic and purāṇic tropes, highlighting how Sultan appropriated avatāric descent, dharmic genealogy, and the Bangla poetic register to present the prophetic chain.

One of the most significant features of Saiyad Sultan's work is his use of the Vaiṣṇava concept of aṃśāvatāra, or partial divine manifestation, to explain Muhammad's primordial relationship with Allah. Through this conceptual framework, Muhammad is presented in terms intelligible to Bengali readers familiar with Indic theological ideas, while his distinctive status within Islamic prophetic history is maintained (2021, pp. 39–40).

Through the Nabīvaṃśa, Saiyad Sultan attempted to localise Islam by presenting Muhammad in the form of Viṣṇu's kalki avatar in a landscape deeply rooted in the traditions of Gauṛiya Vaiṣṇavism. Thus, Sultan portrayed Islam not as a new religion but rather as the local population's longstanding religious tradition. By integrating Hindu deities and sacred texts into Islamic prophetology, Saiyad Sultan implicitly expands the Qur’anic concept of the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab) to encompass the Hindu communities of Bengal.

Irani's contribution is particularly important for reconsidering Roy's concept of syncretism. Whereas Roy emphasises the absorption and reinterpretation of local cultural materials within Bengali Islam, Irani directs attention to the literary and theological strategies through which Islamic knowledge was translated into Bengali. The vernacular text did not merely reflect an already established Muslim identity; it actively participated in constructing the intellectual and religious categories through which Bengali Muslims could understand Islamic sacred history. An example of such an attempt is Sultan's use of the term Prabhu Niranjan, rather than Allah, to refer to the Creator.

The difference between the two approaches should not be overstated. Both recognise the importance of Bengali literary production in the historical formation of Muslim religious culture. Their principal difference concerns how the relationship between Islamic textual authority and indigenous cultural forms should be interpreted. Roy foregrounds cultural mediation and syncretistic formation, while Irani emphasises translation, theological articulation, and the vernacularisation of Islamic salvation history.

Regarding the influence of non-Islamic traditions on Sufism, other scholars, in addition to Roy, Eaton, Stewart, and Irani, have argued that it gradually incorporated Tantric, Yogic, Nātha, and other indigenous practices as it developed in the Indian subcontinent.

Muhammad Enamul Haq (1975), in his A History of Sufi-ism in Bengal, for example, suggests that although the fundamental principles of Sufism in Bengal remained comparable to those of northern India until the sixteenth century, Bengali Sufism subsequently developed closer associations with Tantrikism, Yogism, Nāthism, and other similar systems of indigenous thought and asceticism (p. 52). He identifies conceptual parallels between Sufi understandings of the soul, spiritual discipline, and stages of mystical realisation and corresponding ideas in Hindu and Buddhist traditions. His discussion includes comparisons between the Sufi concepts of rūḥ and al-nafs and the Indic concepts of ātman and citta, as well as between Sufi stages of spiritual realisation and Buddhist accounts of spiritual attainment. Such comparisons draw attention to the intellectual encounters that took place between religious communities in the subcontinent. Nevertheless, in assessing the contributions of Sufis in Bengal, Haq acknowledges that Sufis exerted considerable influence on Vaishnavism, particularly on its concept of prema, or divine love, and that the Vaishnava emphasis on a casteless society appeared to derive from Sufi influence. He maintains, “Growth of cordiality and unity between the Hindus and the Muslims of Bengal is one of the great achievements that the Sufis accomplished in this country” (p. 287).

Abdul Karim (1985) also emphasises the institutional and popular dimensions of Sufism in Bengal. He argues that Muslim rulers, in collaboration with Sufi figures, established mosques, madrasas, and khanqahs, which helped introduce local populations to Islamic teachings and institutions. At the popular level, the authority of pirs and the veneration of their dargahs became central features of Bengali Muslim religious life. Karim associates the popular understanding of pir authority with certain familiar aspects of Hindu and Buddhist religious traditions, including the veneration of spiritual teachers and sacred sites. He suggests that such parallels may have facilitated the acceptance of Sufi figures among populations previously familiar with the authority of Tantric gurus and other religious intermediaries. He observes that the Sufis deeply influenced the masses and that, even at the time of his writing, their dargahs or tombs continued to be visited and venerated by both Muslims and Hindus (p. 160).

These interpretations point to an important distinction between formal Islamic institutions and popular devotional practices. The former provided mechanisms for transmitting scriptural knowledge and normative religious teachings, while the latter offered forms of spiritual guidance, intercession, healing, protection, and communal belonging. This relationship became increasingly contested in subsequent periods.

The accommodationist and locally embedded character of Bengali Muslim religious culture encountered sustained criticism during the nineteenth century. Reformist movements sought to redefine Muslim religious identity by challenging practices they considered incompatible with Islamic scriptural norms. Among the most influential were the Fara'idi movement, the Tariqa-i Muhammadiyya, and the Tayyuni movement.

However, the Fara'idi movement cannot be understood exclusively as a campaign for religious purification, even during the leadership of Haji Shariatullah (d. 1840). Under the leadership of his son Dudu Miyan, it developed into a broader peasant mobilisation against oppressive landlordism and colonial agrarian arrangements. Its appeal among the Muslim peasantry was connected with the social and economic conditions of rural Bengal, particularly the unequal distribution of land and the burdens associated with existing systems of rent and taxation.

The Tariqa-i Muhammadiyya and Tayyuni movements also contributed to debates about Islamic orthodoxy and religious practice. Although they differed in their doctrinal positions, political orientations, and attitudes towards congregational worship, they shared criticisms of certain popular devotional practices. Their disagreements also concerned the legal and political status of British-ruled India and the obligations of Muslims living under non-Muslim political authority (Muinuddin Ahmed Khan, History of the Fara’idi Movement in Bengal (1818–1906), 1965, pp. 89–103).
 
Cover of Rafiuddin Ahmed’s The Bengal Muslims 1871–1906: A Quest for Identity (Oxford University Press, 1996, second edition).

The reformist criticism of shrine-centred practices should therefore be situated within a broader transformation of Muslim religious authority. These movements sought to privilege scriptural interpretation, obligatory religious observance, and reformist scholarship over certain established forms of popular devotional authority. Their criticism did not necessarily eliminate Sufi institutions, but it changed the terms through which shrine veneration and saintly authority were publicly contested.

Rafiuddin Ahmed (1981, p. 106) characterises an important aspect of nineteenth-century Islamic reform in Bengal as an attempt to reject elements of Bengali cultural life that reformers regarded as incompatible with Islam. This observation highlights the tension between locally rooted religious practices and movements seeking to establish more standardised forms of Islamic identity.

The subsequent expansion of Deobandi-oriented institutions of Islamic learning, colonial education, and other reformist organisations further transformed the religious landscape. In the twentieth century, Tablighi Jama'at and other reform-oriented movements contributed to the continuing debate over the legitimacy of popular Sufi practices. In contemporary Bangladesh, these debates are also reflected in the positions of various Islamist and Salafi-oriented groups, including Jamaat-e-Islami and other religious organisations.

In conclusion, we may say that the history of Sufism in the Bengal delta demonstrates that the Islamisation of the region was neither a singular historical event nor a straightforward process of religious conversion. It involved the transformation of landscapes, the expansion of agricultural settlements, the establishment of religious institutions, the development of devotional practices, and the production of vernacular Islamic knowledge. The persistence of shrine-centred religious life alongside reformist challenges demonstrates that the history of Bengali Islam is not merely a history of conversion but also a history of the continuous negotiation of religious identity, authority, and belonging.

Dr Sarwar Alam is currently an Adjunct Professor of Religious Studies at George Mason University, USA. He can be reached at [email protected].

This paper was presented at Harvard University on 21 November 2026 at a symposium hosted by the Nisbaat Center for Sufi Studies in collaboration with the Bangladesh Student Association at Harvard.

He contends that the Sufis' engagement in expanding arable land made Islam synonymous with agrarian growth. In fact, he argues, the growth of Muslim societies correlated with the adoption of sedentary agriculture (1990, p. 35). Thus, Islam was perceived culturally by the local population as a civilisation-building ideology and, as such, was not viewed as an alien tradition (1993, p. 310).

Early pioneers of Islam, both Sufi and non-Sufi, took advantage, in some cases, of the incentives offered by Muslim rulers in the form of land grants for clearing forests to expand rice cultivation. While non-Sufi preachers established mosques and madrasas, Sufi preachers and their followers established not only mosques but also khanqahs and dargahs. These institutions fostered both the formal and spiritual aspects of Islam, and together they contributed to the emergence of an Islamic culture. Alongside the expansion of arable land and the agrarian way of life, a locally structured form of Islam, increasingly infused with the culture of saints and saint veneration, gave rise to large Muslim communities in Bengal (1990, p. 36).
 
The Sixty Dome Mosque in Bagerhat, built by the Sufi saint and general Khan Jahan Ali in the 15th century, stands as a testament to the historical expansion of Islam in the Bengal delta. Photo: Moaz Mahmud/Wikimedia Commons

Muslim rulers, particularly the Mughals, were interested not in religious conversion but rather in revenue extraction through land grant policies aimed at expanding arable land by clearing forests. Eaton observes that Mughal administrators frequently distinguished political governance from religious proselytisation. He observes that Muslim rulers, especially “the Mughals were determined not to allow religion to interfere with their administration in Bengal” (2001, p. 31) and did not promote the conversion of Bengalis to Islam. He holds, “Regarding the religion of Mughal ashraf, three features stand out: (a) a special link with the pan-Indian Chishti Order, (b) a conceptual separation of religion and state, and (c) a disinclination to convert Bengalis to Islam” (2001, p. 28). This interpretation complicates the assumption that Muslim political authority automatically produced religious conversion.

Rafiuddin Ahmed (The Bengali Muslims 1871–1906: A Quest for Identity, 2001, p. 12) similarly emphasises the relationship between Muslim institutional expansion and the acculturation of local cultivating communities. He argues that Muslim rulers established mosques and madrasas, supported Islamic scholars and preachers, endowed religious institutions, and appointed qazis. These developments contributed to the gradual expansion of Muslim society, particularly through the incorporation of new agricultural communities.

Taken together, Eaton and Ahmed demonstrate that the historical formation of Muslim society in Bengal involved more than the preaching of religious doctrines. It was embedded in the transformation of land, settlement, institutions, and everyday social relations. Sufis were important participants in this process, but their activities operated alongside those of rulers, administrators, scholars, merchants, and non-Sufi religious figures.

Ayesha A. Irani's The Muhammad Avatāra: Salvation History, Translation, and the Making of Bengali Islam (2021) extends the discussion of Bengali Islamisation by examining the relationship between translation, religious imagination, and the production of Islamic knowledge. Her study focuses particularly on the seventeenth-century Bengali Muslim poet Saiyad Sultan and his Nabīvaṃśa (The Lineage of the Prophets). Drawing on the Arabo-Persian tradition of the Tales of the Prophets (qisas an-nabiya), the work presents Islamic salvation history through Bengali literary conventions and conceptual frameworks familiar to its audience.

Irani demonstrates that the Nabīvaṃśa reflects extensive intellectual and literary exchanges among Muslim, Vaiṣṇava, Nātha, and haṭhayoga traditions. These exchanges reveal common features shared by both Muslim and non-Muslim communities. As Irani observes, they “share a host of these and other common features—theological, narratological, aesthetic, rhetorical, and linguistic—suggests that they participated in overlapping polysystems of performance and reception, of Sufism, Nātha doctrine, haṭhayoga, and Kṛṣṇa bhakti, of orally and textually, evidence of, among other things, the fluency of the circulation of ideas and peoples in the premodern period” (p. 33).

Irani further interprets the Nabīvaṃśa as an example of what she describes as a "Purāṇa-Korān" tradition. In this literary framework, Saiyad Sultan reconstructs prophetic history through a narrative that incorporates pre-Ādamic prophets, Hindu religious figures, and Indic sacred texts into an Islamic account of salvation. The narrative's recurring motif of the earth's appeal for divine intervention provides a framework for connecting different religious histories and establishing Muhammad's prophetic significance (p. 195). It also illustrates the integration of Qurʾānic and purāṇic tropes, highlighting how Sultan appropriated avatāric descent, dharmic genealogy, and the Bangla poetic register to present the prophetic chain.

One of the most significant features of Saiyad Sultan's work is his use of the Vaiṣṇava concept of aṃśāvatāra, or partial divine manifestation, to explain Muhammad's primordial relationship with Allah. Through this conceptual framework, Muhammad is presented in terms intelligible to Bengali readers familiar with Indic theological ideas, while his distinctive status within Islamic prophetic history is maintained (2021, pp. 39–40).

Through the Nabīvaṃśa, Saiyad Sultan attempted to localise Islam by presenting Muhammad in the form of Viṣṇu's kalki avatar in a landscape deeply rooted in the traditions of Gauṛiya Vaiṣṇavism. Thus, Sultan portrayed Islam not as a new religion but rather as the local population's longstanding religious tradition. By integrating Hindu deities and sacred texts into Islamic prophetology, Saiyad Sultan implicitly expands the Qur’anic concept of the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab) to encompass the Hindu communities of Bengal.

Irani's contribution is particularly important for reconsidering Roy's concept of syncretism. Whereas Roy emphasises the absorption and reinterpretation of local cultural materials within Bengali Islam, Irani directs attention to the literary and theological strategies through which Islamic knowledge was translated into Bengali. The vernacular text did not merely reflect an already established Muslim identity; it actively participated in constructing the intellectual and religious categories through which Bengali Muslims could understand Islamic sacred history. An example of such an attempt is Sultan's use of the term Prabhu Niranjan, rather than Allah, to refer to the Creator.

The difference between the two approaches should not be overstated. Both recognise the importance of Bengali literary production in the historical formation of Muslim religious culture. Their principal difference concerns how the relationship between Islamic textual authority and indigenous cultural forms should be interpreted. Roy foregrounds cultural mediation and syncretistic formation, while Irani emphasises translation, theological articulation, and the vernacularisation of Islamic salvation history.

Regarding the influence of non-Islamic traditions on Sufism, other scholars, in addition to Roy, Eaton, Stewart, and Irani, have argued that it gradually incorporated Tantric, Yogic, Nātha, and other indigenous practices as it developed in the Indian subcontinent.

Muhammad Enamul Haq (1975), in his A History of Sufi-ism in Bengal, for example, suggests that although the fundamental principles of Sufism in Bengal remained comparable to those of northern India until the sixteenth century, Bengali Sufism subsequently developed closer associations with Tantrikism, Yogism, Nāthism, and other similar systems of indigenous thought and asceticism (p. 52). He identifies conceptual parallels between Sufi understandings of the soul, spiritual discipline, and stages of mystical realisation and corresponding ideas in Hindu and Buddhist traditions. His discussion includes comparisons between the Sufi concepts of rūḥ and al-nafs and the Indic concepts of ātman and citta, as well as between Sufi stages of spiritual realisation and Buddhist accounts of spiritual attainment. Such comparisons draw attention to the intellectual encounters that took place between religious communities in the subcontinent. Nevertheless, in assessing the contributions of Sufis in Bengal, Haq acknowledges that Sufis exerted considerable influence on Vaishnavism, particularly on its concept of prema, or divine love, and that the Vaishnava emphasis on a casteless society appeared to derive from Sufi influence. He maintains, “Growth of cordiality and unity between the Hindus and the Muslims of Bengal is one of the great achievements that the Sufis accomplished in this country” (p. 287).

Abdul Karim (1985) also emphasises the institutional and popular dimensions of Sufism in Bengal. He argues that Muslim rulers, in collaboration with Sufi figures, established mosques, madrasas, and khanqahs, which helped introduce local populations to Islamic teachings and institutions. At the popular level, the authority of pirs and the veneration of their dargahs became central features of Bengali Muslim religious life. Karim associates the popular understanding of pir authority with certain familiar aspects of Hindu and Buddhist religious traditions, including the veneration of spiritual teachers and sacred sites. He suggests that such parallels may have facilitated the acceptance of Sufi figures among populations previously familiar with the authority of Tantric gurus and other religious intermediaries. He observes that the Sufis deeply influenced the masses and that, even at the time of his writing, their dargahs or tombs continued to be visited and venerated by both Muslims and Hindus (p. 160).

These interpretations point to an important distinction between formal Islamic institutions and popular devotional practices. The former provided mechanisms for transmitting scriptural knowledge and normative religious teachings, while the latter offered forms of spiritual guidance, intercession, healing, protection, and communal belonging. This relationship became increasingly contested in subsequent periods.

The accommodationist and locally embedded character of Bengali Muslim religious culture encountered sustained criticism during the nineteenth century. Reformist movements sought to redefine Muslim religious identity by challenging practices they considered incompatible with Islamic scriptural norms. Among the most influential were the Fara'idi movement, the Tariqa-i Muhammadiyya, and the Tayyuni movement.

However, the Fara'idi movement cannot be understood exclusively as a campaign for religious purification, even during the leadership of Haji Shariatullah (d. 1840). Under the leadership of his son Dudu Miyan, it developed into a broader peasant mobilisation against oppressive landlordism and colonial agrarian arrangements. Its appeal among the Muslim peasantry was connected with the social and economic conditions of rural Bengal, particularly the unequal distribution of land and the burdens associated with existing systems of rent and taxation.

The Tariqa-i Muhammadiyya and Tayyuni movements also contributed to debates about Islamic orthodoxy and religious practice. Although they differed in their doctrinal positions, political orientations, and attitudes towards congregational worship, they shared criticisms of certain popular devotional practices. Their disagreements also concerned the legal and political status of British-ruled India and the obligations of Muslims living under non-Muslim political authority (Muinuddin Ahmed Khan, History of the Fara’idi Movement in Bengal (1818–1906), 1965, pp. 89–103).
 
Cover of Rafiuddin Ahmed’s The Bengal Muslims 1871–1906: A Quest for Identity (Oxford University Press, 1996, second edition).

The reformist criticism of shrine-centred practices should therefore be situated within a broader transformation of Muslim religious authority. These movements sought to privilege scriptural interpretation, obligatory religious observance, and reformist scholarship over certain established forms of popular devotional authority. Their criticism did not necessarily eliminate Sufi institutions, but it changed the terms through which shrine veneration and saintly authority were publicly contested.

Rafiuddin Ahmed (1981, p. 106) characterises an important aspect of nineteenth-century Islamic reform in Bengal as an attempt to reject elements of Bengali cultural life that reformers regarded as incompatible with Islam. This observation highlights the tension between locally rooted religious practices and movements seeking to establish more standardised forms of Islamic identity.

The subsequent expansion of Deobandi-oriented institutions of Islamic learning, colonial education, and other reformist organisations further transformed the religious landscape. In the twentieth century, Tablighi Jama'at and other reform-oriented movements contributed to the continuing debate over the legitimacy of popular Sufi practices. In contemporary Bangladesh, these debates are also reflected in the positions of various Islamist and Salafi-oriented groups, including Jamaat-e-Islami and other religious organisations.

In conclusion, we may say that the history of Sufism in the Bengal delta demonstrates that the Islamisation of the region was neither a singular historical event nor a straightforward process of religious conversion. It involved the transformation of landscapes, the expansion of agricultural settlements, the establishment of religious institutions, the development of devotional practices, and the production of vernacular Islamic knowledge. The persistence of shrine-centred religious life alongside reformist challenges demonstrates that the history of Bengali Islam is not merely a history of conversion but also a history of the continuous negotiation of religious identity, authority, and belonging.

item.description:
For generations, Bangladesh’s medical and legal systems placed the burden of proving credibility on rape survivors. In 2018, a landmark High Court ruling challenged this culture of suspicion. As the world marks the 16 Days of Activism in 2026 under the theme “Ensure justice, protect survivors, end impunity”, we revisit the struggle to secure the ban on the two-finger test and examine the challenges that remain in translating legal reform into practice.

Imagine a woman who has survived rape. Reporting it was not easy. She had to find the courage to tell others what happened to her body, and then to keep telling it, again and again, to the police, to doctors and to lawyers.

What followed was often another ordeal. A court wanted evidence, so she was sent for a medical examination. This is called a medico-legal examination, and the doctor writes down the findings in a certificate that goes to the court. Later, at the trial, the lawyer for the accused is allowed to question her. This is called cross-examination.

In Bangladesh, for a very long time, both of these steps could involve the same question: was she “habituated to sex”? In plain words, had she had sex before? A doctor might record it in the certificate. A lawyer might ask it aloud in court.

It may sound like a small detail. It is not. A rape case has to answer one question: did she agree to what happened that day? Consent belongs to that moment and to that person’s choice. What she did before says nothing about it. A woman can be married, can have a partner, can earn her living through sex, and still be raped. Yet a finding or a question about her past quietly moves the court’s attention away from what the perpetrator did and towards how the woman has lived. It invites the court to doubt her when it should be asking what was done to her. Neither medical findings about a woman’s sexual history nor questions about her past can establish whether she consented to the sexual act in question. Yet for decades, both practices remained routine in rape investigations and trials in Bangladesh.
Although the two-finger test was banned in 2018, the legal provision that allowed a rape survivor’s character to be questioned in court remained in force until 2022. Photo: AI generated

The challenge to this practice began with a simple but disturbing question. Does this imply that a person who is habituated to sex cannot be a victim of rape? Can a sex worker not be raped? Are sex workers not entitled to justice? Can a married woman not be a victim of intimate partner violence?

A colonial legacy of questioning women

Women in Bangladesh did not encounter this suspicion for the first time in an examination room. It had been written into law and taught in medical manuals. The two-finger test was one expression of a wider pattern in which the burden of proving credibility fell on the woman, while responsibility for violence did not fall on the perpetrator.

The roots of the test in the Indian subcontinent, including present-day Bangladesh, lie in British medical jurisprudence. Manuals such as Norman Chevers’s A Manual of Medical Jurisprudence for India (1870) and later texts by Isador B. Lyon became authoritative references for medico-legal procedures. Historian Hanne Blank reminds us in Virgin: The Untouched History that virginity testing is neither unique to South Asia nor confined to rape trials. It has appeared across cultures and eras. But within the colonial legal-medical framework, it was codified and legitimised here as a tool to question survivors rather than to support them.

The law reinforced it. Section 155(4) of the Evidence Act 1872, rooted in Victorian ideas about sexuality, said that when a person was prosecuted for rape, “it may be shown that the prosecutrix is of generally immoral character”. The underlying assumption was that women might fabricate allegations of rape, so their sexual histories could be used to assess their credibility.

The suspicion has older roots still. In Satirai Kebol Dhorshito Hoy (roughly, “Only the Chaste Are Raped”), her 2015 study for BLAST of how Section 155(4) worked in practice, researcher Fatema Sultana Shubhra points to the Victorian ideas about sexuality that shaped the 1872 law. In that view, a respectable woman was not supposed to feel sexual desire at all, and her duty was to serve her husband. Desire was seen as a male trait or as the mark of women of the lower classes, such as sex workers. A woman who showed it could be treated as unwell.

Shubhra argues that this notion of purity did not disappear with the departure of the colonial rulers. She also notes that the seventeenth-century English judge Matthew Hale described rape as a charge that was easy to make, hard to prove and harder still to defend against, and the rape trial as one in which the complainant herself ends up being tried. According to Shubhra, this view continues to shape the legal culture surrounding rape cases.

The two-finger test became part of this culture of suspicion. By examining the hymen and assessing vaginal laxity, practitioners sought to label women as “habituated to sexual intercourse”. The language pulled attention away from the one question that mattered, consent, and towards the supposed morality of the woman who had come forward.

The questions point to those who faced the heaviest scrutiny: married women, sex workers and anyone whose life did not match what society expected. None of these circumstances can establish consent to a sexual act.

In 2022, Section 155(4) was repealed through an amendment to the Evidence Act. That was an important change, and it came four years after the High Court ban in 2018. But habits within institutions do not disappear just because a provision is deleted.

What the test is and why it fails

A “per vaginum” or two-finger test is an intrusive physical examination in which a doctor inserts two fingers into the vagina of a rape survivor to check whether the hymen is intact and to assess the size of the vaginal opening and vaginal laxity.

None of this proves or disproves rape. Neither the state of the hymen nor vaginal laxity can scientifically establish whether sexual assault occurred or consent was given. Dr Ruchira Tabassum Naved of icddr,b, one of the petitioners, explains that laxity varies from person to person and that the test rests on the faulty notion that a lack of resistance proves consent. But rape often takes place through coercion, intimidation and threats, which can also be implicit, rendering a woman unable to resist. Injuries can typically be found in 70 percent of rape cases, and rape does not involve only the vagina.
The first page of the High Court judgment of April 12, 2018, banning the two-finger test for rape survivors. The court described the practice as “unscientific, inconclusive, and degrading, with no forensic value”.

Advocates describe the practice in three words:

  • Unscientific: it has no forensic value in proving or disproving rape.

  • Traumatic: it is often conducted without consent and has been described as a form of secondary rape.

  • Humiliating: it perpetuates the myth that women lie about rape and places an unfair burden of proof on survivors.

Even as a means of gathering evidence, the examination is questionable, since it usually takes place too late from a medical standpoint. And it places an additional burden on women who already live with the fear of violence from partners and of ridicule and retribution from families and communities.

How the ban was won

Between 2010 and 2014, BLAST (Bangladesh Legal Aid and Services Trust) was part of the SAFE project, a joint effort with four other organisations that aimed to reduce gender-based violence against young women and girls in urban slums. But the advocacy, Akhter says, grew out of BLAST’s everyday work with survivors.

“We began to notice that the cases of sexual violence survivors who sought BLAST’s assistance were either failing to secure any remedy or were becoming entangled in prolonged delays,” she recalls. “We felt compelled to investigate why this was happening.”

Sixty-five cases were selected for in-depth study. Around 2009–10, Fatema Shubhra of Jagannath University reviewed them. Her report, initially unpublished, later became the basis of a book she published in 2015. It pointed to two failures: the medico-legal examination and the degrading cross-examination of survivors in court.

Indian consultant Ashmita Basu, who reviewed more than 50 of the 65 cases, found that the test was being applied indiscriminately to survivors ranging from children to married women. Legal intern Sylvie McCallum Rougerie visited the facilities herself and observed the examinations. She confirmed that they violated the human rights of the women being examined.

In October 2013, BLAST joined a coalition of rights and development organisations and two experts, Dr Ruchira Naved and Dr Mobarak Hossain Khan, to file a writ petition challenging the test. Then came the slow work of persuasion. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare formed committees to draft medico-legal guidelines. Many forensic experts, those involved recall, “could not be persuaded” at first, so the conversations continued and later extended to gynaecologists.

Professor Dr Gulshan Ara of BIRDEM General Hospital told them plainly that the test had no scientific basis. In 2017, five forensic experts stated that it was unscientific and unnecessary.

“The journey from 2013 to 2018 was not easy,” the advocates recall. “Many individuals had to be convinced to appear before the court.”

Key moments

  • 8 October 2013: BLAST, together with Ain O Salish Kendra, Bangladesh Mahila Parishad, BRAC, Manusher Jonno Foundation, Naripokkho, Dr Ruchira Tabassum Naved and Dr Mobarak Hossain Khan, files a writ petition (WP No. 10663/2013) challenging the validity of the test.

  • 10 October 2013: The High Court issues a Rule Nisi and an interim direction to develop comprehensive guidelines for examining and treating survivors of rape and sexual violence.

  • 7 August 2016: The High Court requires forensic experts to give their opinions on the test.

  • 16 August 2017: Experts state that the test is unscientific and unnecessary.

  • April 2018: The High Court bans the test.

  • 21 July 2019: A government circular is issued in light of the directives.

In April 2018, the bench comprising Justice Gobinda Chandra Tagore and Justice AKM Shahidul Huq held that the test was “not scientific, reliable and valid” and violated survivors’ fundamental rights under Articles 27, 28, 31, 35(5), 39(1) and 43(b) of the Constitution. The practice was described as “unscientific, inconclusive, and degrading with no forensic value”. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare chose not to appeal and began implementing a new medico-legal protocol.
Cover of Satirai Kebol Dhorshito Hoy (“Only the Chaste Are Raped”), Fatema Sultana Shubhra’s 2015 study for BLAST, which warned that banning the two-finger test alone might not end institutional victim-blaming.

Eight directives

The decision went beyond prohibiting the test. The court issued eight directives intended to improve the medical and legal response to rape survivors.

The court ordered that the government’s Health Response to Gender-based Violence protocols be made available to forensic experts, doctors, police officers, public prosecutors and other relevant professionals. Doctors and forensic experts were instructed not to use degrading expressions such as “habituated to sexual intercourse” in medical certificates and not to ask about a survivor’s past sexual experiences. Cases requiring deep intravaginal examinations for medical reasons should be referred to gynaecologists.

For children and young girls, per speculum examinations are not mandatory where there is no history of penetration or visible injury. The bimanual test, which is unrelated to the two-finger test and is used for obstetric and gynaecological purposes, should not be performed on rape survivors.

Other directives call for trained doctors and nurses, preferably female physicians, with female police officers or female relatives present during examinations to ensure that the survivor’s privacy is protected. The court also instructed the Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Tribunal to prevent lawyers from asking degrading questions that are unnecessary for establishing the facts of the alleged rape.

Taken together, the directives rest on one principle: the medical and legal systems must protect survivors’ dignity rather than subject them to further humiliation.

A ban on paper, a practice in progress

A ruling is not the same as a change in the clinic. In July 2019, a government circular was issued in light of the directives. Yet in April 2023, the Advancing Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (AdSEARCH) project of icddr,b began a study of how the ban was actually being implemented.

Completed in September 2024, the study covered eight public health facilities and included interviews with lawyers and NGO staff in Dhaka, Dinajpur and Rangpur. The study, along with interviews with those who led the legal fight, identified persistent barriers:

  • Lack of training: awareness of the protocols among police officers, medical professionals and local lawyers remains inadequate.

  • Lack of information: survivors and their families are often unaware of the ban.

  • Legal arrangements: there are no penalties for violating the protocol, which weakens enforcement.

Advocate Kamrun Nahar of Naripokkho says the 2018 ruling “has not yet been effectively disseminated across all the relevant sectors”. She proposes presenting the eight directives in a concise booklet written in plain language and distributing it widely.

Advocate Md. Shahinuzzaman of Ain O Salish Kendra puts the legal position plainly: since the High Court has ruled, compliance is mandatory, and the test cannot be conducted under any circumstances. Nor can a lawyer present its results as evidence of rape in court.

A warning from 2015 now reads like a forecast. Writing three years before the High Court ban, Shubhra cautioned that scrapping the two-finger test alone might not be enough. If Section 155(4) remained in the law, she warned, another medico-legal method could take its place and give the idea of the “immoral” woman a scientific basis, keeping the same suspicion alive through another such test. Her first recommendation was to repeal the clause entirely.

The test was banned in 2018, but the law that allowed a survivor’s character to be put on trial remained in place until 2022. The gap revealed how legal reform can move faster than the institutions and assumptions it seeks to change.
Protesters hold candles and placards demanding justice for rape survivors and an end to victim-blaming. A survivor’s sexual history can never be grounds for dismissing a rape allegation. Photo: Star

The court ended the test in 2018. The clause itself was repealed in 2022. For four years, then, the test was banned while the rule that allowed a survivor’s character to be put on trial was still on the books. That gap is a reminder that a ban is only a beginning. The suspicion underlying the test has to be removed from the law and from the habits of the institutions that apply it.

The steps needed to strengthen implementation are practical and achievable: make information easily available to survivors, display the guidelines in forensic centres, and organise specialised training for doctors, police officers and lawyers.

Beyond the examination room, Dr Naved reminds us that the legal framework still leaves important gaps. Anal, oral and other forms of rape are overlooked in the legislation, and marital rape remains a “huge caveat”.

The two-finger test was imported with a presumption: that a woman accusing a man of rape must first prove she deserves to be believed. The 2018 ruling rejected that presumption in the one place where it was most invasive. Giving effect to that rejection in every clinic, police station and courtroom is the work that remains.

A judgment can prohibit a practice, but only institutions can ensure that it does not return in another form. The responsibility now lies with the health and justice systems to make the court’s directives part of everyday practice.

Prior sexual activity can never be a reason to dismiss a rape allegation. And no survivor should have to endure degrading examinations, questioning or suspicion in the name of an inherited law.

UN Women’s theme for this year’s 16 Days of Activism is “UNiTE to End Violence Against Women and Girls: Ensure justice, protect survivors, end impunity”. The story of the two-finger test is one of a court that delivered justice, directives that promised protection, and a protocol whose implementation still lacks clear mechanisms for accountability.

A.S.M. Riad Arif and Anubhab Chakraborty work at the International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research, Bangladesh (icddr,b).

This article draws on A Collective Effort to Record the Historical Milestones of the Two-Finger Test Ban (AdSEARCH by icddr,b, April 2026).

The language pulled attention away from the one question that mattered, consent, and towards the supposed morality of the woman who had come forward.

The questions point to those who faced the heaviest scrutiny: married women, sex workers and anyone whose life did not match what society expected. None of these circumstances can establish consent to a sexual act.

In 2022, Section 155(4) was repealed through an amendment to the Evidence Act. That was an important change, and it came four years after the High Court ban in 2018. But habits within institutions do not disappear just because a provision is deleted.

What the test is and why it fails

A “per vaginum” or two-finger test is an intrusive physical examination in which a doctor inserts two fingers into the vagina of a rape survivor to check whether the hymen is intact and to assess the size of the vaginal opening and vaginal laxity.

None of this proves or disproves rape. Neither the state of the hymen nor vaginal laxity can scientifically establish whether sexual assault occurred or consent was given. Dr Ruchira Tabassum Naved of icddr,b, one of the petitioners, explains that laxity varies from person to person and that the test rests on the faulty notion that a lack of resistance proves consent. But rape often takes place through coercion, intimidation and threats, which can also be implicit, rendering a woman unable to resist. Injuries can typically be found in 70 percent of rape cases, and rape does not involve only the vagina.
The first page of the High Court judgment of April 12, 2018, banning the two-finger test for rape survivors. The court described the practice as “unscientific, inconclusive, and degrading, with no forensic value”.

Advocates describe the practice in three words:

  • Unscientific: it has no forensic value in proving or disproving rape.

  • Traumatic: it is often conducted without consent and has been described as a form of secondary rape.

  • Humiliating: it perpetuates the myth that women lie about rape and places an unfair burden of proof on survivors.

Even as a means of gathering evidence, the examination is questionable, since it usually takes place too late from a medical standpoint. And it places an additional burden on women who already live with the fear of violence from partners and of ridicule and retribution from families and communities.

How the ban was won

Between 2010 and 2014, BLAST (Bangladesh Legal Aid and Services Trust) was part of the SAFE project, a joint effort with four other organisations that aimed to reduce gender-based violence against young women and girls in urban slums. But the advocacy, Akhter says, grew out of BLAST’s everyday work with survivors.

“We began to notice that the cases of sexual violence survivors who sought BLAST’s assistance were either failing to secure any remedy or were becoming entangled in prolonged delays,” she recalls. “We felt compelled to investigate why this was happening.”

Sixty-five cases were selected for in-depth study. Around 2009–10, Fatema Shubhra of Jagannath University reviewed them. Her report, initially unpublished, later became the basis of a book she published in 2015. It pointed to two failures: the medico-legal examination and the degrading cross-examination of survivors in court.

Indian consultant Ashmita Basu, who reviewed more than 50 of the 65 cases, found that the test was being applied indiscriminately to survivors ranging from children to married women. Legal intern Sylvie McCallum Rougerie visited the facilities herself and observed the examinations. She confirmed that they violated the human rights of the women being examined.

In October 2013, BLAST joined a coalition of rights and development organisations and two experts, Dr Ruchira Naved and Dr Mobarak Hossain Khan, to file a writ petition challenging the test. Then came the slow work of persuasion. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare formed committees to draft medico-legal guidelines. Many forensic experts, those involved recall, “could not be persuaded” at first, so the conversations continued and later extended to gynaecologists.

Professor Dr Gulshan Ara of BIRDEM General Hospital told them plainly that the test had no scientific basis. In 2017, five forensic experts stated that it was unscientific and unnecessary.

“The journey from 2013 to 2018 was not easy,” the advocates recall. “Many individuals had to be convinced to appear before the court.”

Key moments

  • 8 October 2013: BLAST, together with Ain O Salish Kendra, Bangladesh Mahila Parishad, BRAC, Manusher Jonno Foundation, Naripokkho, Dr Ruchira Tabassum Naved and Dr Mobarak Hossain Khan, files a writ petition (WP No. 10663/2013) challenging the validity of the test.

  • 10 October 2013: The High Court issues a Rule Nisi and an interim direction to develop comprehensive guidelines for examining and treating survivors of rape and sexual violence.

  • 7 August 2016: The High Court requires forensic experts to give their opinions on the test.

  • 16 August 2017: Experts state that the test is unscientific and unnecessary.

  • April 2018: The High Court bans the test.

  • 21 July 2019: A government circular is issued in light of the directives.

In April 2018, the bench comprising Justice Gobinda Chandra Tagore and Justice AKM Shahidul Huq held that the test was “not scientific, reliable and valid” and violated survivors’ fundamental rights under Articles 27, 28, 31, 35(5), 39(1) and 43(b) of the Constitution. The practice was described as “unscientific, inconclusive, and degrading with no forensic value”. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare chose not to appeal and began implementing a new medico-legal protocol.
Cover of Satirai Kebol Dhorshito Hoy (“Only the Chaste Are Raped”), Fatema Sultana Shubhra’s 2015 study for BLAST, which warned that banning the two-finger test alone might not end institutional victim-blaming.

Eight directives

The decision went beyond prohibiting the test. The court issued eight directives intended to improve the medical and legal response to rape survivors.

The court ordered that the government’s Health Response to Gender-based Violence protocols be made available to forensic experts, doctors, police officers, public prosecutors and other relevant professionals. Doctors and forensic experts were instructed not to use degrading expressions such as “habituated to sexual intercourse” in medical certificates and not to ask about a survivor’s past sexual experiences. Cases requiring deep intravaginal examinations for medical reasons should be referred to gynaecologists.

For children and young girls, per speculum examinations are not mandatory where there is no history of penetration or visible injury. The bimanual test, which is unrelated to the two-finger test and is used for obstetric and gynaecological purposes, should not be performed on rape survivors.

Other directives call for trained doctors and nurses, preferably female physicians, with female police officers or female relatives present during examinations to ensure that the survivor’s privacy is protected. The court also instructed the Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Tribunal to prevent lawyers from asking degrading questions that are unnecessary for establishing the facts of the alleged rape.

Taken together, the directives rest on one principle: the medical and legal systems must protect survivors’ dignity rather than subject them to further humiliation.

A ban on paper, a practice in progress

A ruling is not the same as a change in the clinic. In July 2019, a government circular was issued in light of the directives. Yet in April 2023, the Advancing Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (AdSEARCH) project of icddr,b began a study of how the ban was actually being implemented.

Completed in September 2024, the study covered eight public health facilities and included interviews with lawyers and NGO staff in Dhaka, Dinajpur and Rangpur. The study, along with interviews with those who led the legal fight, identified persistent barriers:

  • Lack of training: awareness of the protocols among police officers, medical professionals and local lawyers remains inadequate.

  • Lack of information: survivors and their families are often unaware of the ban.

  • Legal arrangements: there are no penalties for violating the protocol, which weakens enforcement.

Advocate Kamrun Nahar of Naripokkho says the 2018 ruling “has not yet been effectively disseminated across all the relevant sectors”. She proposes presenting the eight directives in a concise booklet written in plain language and distributing it widely.

Advocate Md. Shahinuzzaman of Ain O Salish Kendra puts the legal position plainly: since the High Court has ruled, compliance is mandatory, and the test cannot be conducted under any circumstances. Nor can a lawyer present its results as evidence of rape in court.

A warning from 2015 now reads like a forecast. Writing three years before the High Court ban, Shubhra cautioned that scrapping the two-finger test alone might not be enough. If Section 155(4) remained in the law, she warned, another medico-legal method could take its place and give the idea of the “immoral” woman a scientific basis, keeping the same suspicion alive through another such test. Her first recommendation was to repeal the clause entirely.

The test was banned in 2018, but the law that allowed a survivor’s character to be put on trial remained in place until 2022. The gap revealed how legal reform can move faster than the institutions and assumptions it seeks to change.
Protesters hold candles and placards demanding justice for rape survivors and an end to victim-blaming. A survivor’s sexual history can never be grounds for dismissing a rape allegation. Photo: Star

The court ended the test in 2018. The clause itself was repealed in 2022. For four years, then, the test was banned while the rule that allowed a survivor’s character to be put on trial was still on the books. That gap is a reminder that a ban is only a beginning. The suspicion underlying the test has to be removed from the law and from the habits of the institutions that apply it.

The steps needed to strengthen implementation are practical and achievable: make information easily available to survivors, display the guidelines in forensic centres, and organise specialised training for doctors, police officers and lawyers.

Beyond the examination room, Dr Naved reminds us that the legal framework still leaves important gaps. Anal, oral and other forms of rape are overlooked in the legislation, and marital rape remains a “huge caveat”.

The two-finger test was imported with a presumption: that a woman accusing a man of rape must first prove she deserves to be believed. The 2018 ruling rejected that presumption in the one place where it was most invasive. Giving effect to that rejection in every clinic, police station and courtroom is the work that remains.

A judgment can prohibit a practice, but only institutions can ensure that it does not return in another form. The responsibility now lies with the health and justice systems to make the court’s directives part of everyday practice.

Prior sexual activity can never be a reason to dismiss a rape allegation. And no survivor should have to endure degrading examinations, questioning or suspicion in the name of an inherited law.

UN Women’s theme for this year’s 16 Days of Activism is “UNiTE to End Violence Against Women and Girls: Ensure justice, protect survivors, end impunity”. The story of the two-finger test is one of a court that delivered justice, directives that promised protection, and a protocol whose implementation still lacks clear mechanisms for accountability.
